blocks.title: Why Build a RAG App with LangChain matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A LangChain docs assistant answers support questions but often cites the wrong page. The learner's job is not to memorize Build a RAG App with LangChain; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved faithful answer rate on support questions.

Running case: RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Build a RAG App with LangChain matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Build a RAG App with LangChain matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure faithful answer rate on support questions on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check

spans.text: Scenario: A LangChain docs assistant answers support questions but often cites the wrong page. The team wants to improve faithful answer rate on support questions, but it has already seen this failure: the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Question: "Can I get a refund after 35 days if I lost my invoice?" The answer must cite the exact policy chunk, not a plausible refund rule remembered by the model.

Artifact: RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check. It specifies loaders, chunk metadata, retriever settings, prompt contract, citation format, and a faithfulness check for faithful answer rate on support questions.
Worked output: retrieve policy-refunds-v3 section 4, quote "30 days" and "invoice id required", answer that the request probably fails the policy, and link the source chunk used.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: RAG reviewer. Context: A LangChain docs assistant answers support questions but often cites the wrong page. Task: inspect RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check. Require a user question, retrieved chunks with source ids, final answer, and a claim-by-claim support check. Constraints: do not allow claims that are absent from retrieved chunks; flag stale or missing metadata. Output: {question, retrieved_sources, answer, unsupported_claims, release_decision}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Build a RAG App with LangChain to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

Mechanism means separating retrieval quality from answer quality: did the system fetch the right evidence, and did the model stay faithful to that evidence?

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: faithful answer rate on support questions becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Build a RAG App with LangChain design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: Retrieved chunks mention the right keyword but not the answer-bearing paragraph.
The answer is relevant but unfaithful: it adds a policy or fact not present in the retrieved evidence.
Metadata is missing, so citations cannot be checked or reranked later.
The broad warning sign: faithful answer rate on support questions gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

nodes.relevance: It helps the learner improve faithful answer rate on support questions while avoiding the failure: the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks.
nodes.orient: Apply solo: Hardening path connects Build a RAG App with LangChain to the running artifact and failure test.

checklist.label: Can you state the concrete user problem without buzzwords?
Does the artifact show input, evidence or state, decision, output, and owner?
Can you measure faithful answer rate on support questions on realistic cases?
Does a test reproduce this failure: the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks?
Is the next rung clear after the first reliable version?

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page release-ready plan for RAG chain with retriever, prompt, citation contract, and faithfulness check. Include: the user problem, realistic input, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (faithful answer rate on support questions), failure case (the generated answer uses a plausible policy not present in retrieved chunks), owner, and the next rung after this lesson.
